blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
Subject indexing—the process of determining what a work
is about, selecting appropriate controlled vocabulary terms,
and encoding them as subject access fields in a bibliographic
record—remains one of the most time-consuming and cogni-
tively demanding components of library cataloging. It requires
knowledge of a controlled vocabulary exceeding one million
authorized headings, fluency with a complex set of policy doc-
uments (the Subject Headings Manual), and the professional
judgment to balance specificity, depth of indexing, and end-
user discoverability. The complexity of the Library of Cong

summary.text: Introduction. Subject indexing with the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) requires knowledge of a vocabulary of over a million authorised headings, fluency in the Subject Headings Manual, and judgment about specificity and depth. Catalogers need years of training to build complex subject strings independently, and often get none, relying on existing records as examples (Chow and colleagues, 2024). The resulting bottleneck has produced cataloguing backlogs worldwide, leaving new materials undiscoverable (Tang and Jiang, 2025).
Only the section number 1.1.1 (the start of the literature review), with no other text.

blocks.title: Traditional Machine Learning Approaches
blocks.content:
Efforts to automate subject indexing predate the current genera-
tion of large language models. National libraries have pursued
machine learning solutions for over a decade, typically framing
the task as an extreme multi-label text classification (XMTC)
problem in which documents must be assigned labels from a
vocabulary of tens or hundreds of thousands of controlled terms
(D’Souza et al., 2026).
The National Library of Estonia developed Kratt, a prototype
automatic subject indexing tool that used page-level logistic
regression classifiers to assign terms from the Estonian Sub-
ject Thesaurus

summary.text: Literature review, traditional machine-learning approaches. National libraries have treated subject indexing as extreme multi-label text classification (XMTC) over vocabularies of tens or hundreds of thousands of terms. Estonia's Kratt used page-level logistic regression and indexed a book in about a minute, 10–15 times faster than catalogers, but professionals rated its subjects unsatisfactory, and its training labels were very sparse (median label frequency 2). Finland's Annif toolkit combines XMTC algorithms (Omikuji/Bonsai, MLLM lexical matching, XTransformer) into ensembles and is used by several European national libraries. The TIB-SID corpus of 136,000 records with GND subjects shows the structural problem: vocabularies have extreme long-tail distributions because headings are designed to be specific. The block also carries the arXiv identifier (cs.DL, 5 May 2026).

blocks.title: Front matter
blocks.content:
A Skill-Based Agentic Pipeline for Library of Congress Subject Indexing
Eric H. C. Chow
School of Humanities, The University of Hong Kong
eric.chow@hku.hk
Abstract
This paper presents a modular AI agentic skill pipeline for au-
tomating subject indexing with Library of Congress Subject
Headings (LCSH). Subject indexing—the process of analyzing
a work’s aboutness, selecting controlled vocabulary terms, and
encoding them as MARC 21 subject access fields—is one of the
most time-consuming components of library cataloging. The
system decomposes this process into four discrete, sequentially
executed

summary.text: Title, author and abstract of Eric H. C. Chow (School of Humanities, University of Hong Kong), "A Skill-Based Agentic Pipeline for Library of Congress Subject Indexing". Subject indexing, analysing what a work is about, choosing controlled-vocabulary terms and encoding them as MARC 21 subject fields, is among the most time-consuming parts of cataloguing. The system splits it into four agent skills run in sequence (conceptual analysis, quantitative filtering, authority validation, MARC field synthesis), each encoding rules from the Library of Congress Subject Headings Manual (SHM) and subject-analysis theory. It was evaluated on ten titles whose existing headings were taken from the Harvard Library bibliographic dataset. The author reports strong conceptual alignment with professional practice, with differences in specificity, subdivision practice, and the agent's adherence to the 2026 LC policy replacing form subdivisions ($v) with LCGFT 655 fields.

blocks.title: Large Language Models for Subject Indexing
blocks.content:
The emergence of generative AI has prompted a distinct line of
investigation. Brzustowicz (2023) conducted early experiments
testing ChatGPT’s ability to generate complete MARC records.
The results showed that ChatGPT could produce records com-
parable to those created by professional catalogers for basic
metadata fields (title, author, publisher), and could even gener-
ate original records for items without existing WorldCat entries.
However, notable discrepancies emerged in the assignment of
subject access points, suggesting that while LLMs internalize
general cataloging patterns from their

summary.text: LLMs for subject indexing. Brzustowicz (2023) found ChatGPT could produce MARC records comparable to professionals' for basic fields but diverged on subject access points. Chow and colleagues (2024) had ChatGPT assign LCSH to 30 theses: only about half the headings were valid and specific enough, with invented or colloquial terms, though the run cost about $0.25 and three minutes, and refining an AI suggestion was seen as easier than starting from scratch. Tang and Jiang (2025) report 26–35% alignment with human LCSH in one evaluation and propose validating AI candidates against the LC Linked Data Service through MCP. In the SemEval-2025 LLMs4Subjects task (14 teams, GND subjects, bilingual TIB records, quantitative scores plus review by 17 specialists in 28 disciplines), the top all-subjects system was Annif, which used LLMs only for translation and synthetic data, and the organisers judged the advantage of LLMs over traditional methods debatable.

blocks.title: Present Contribution
blocks.content:
The existing literature reveals a consistent pattern: AI systems
can identify relevant topics in a document, but they struggle to
translate those topics into properly constructed LCSH strings
that comply with the Subject Headings Manual. The accu-
racy failures documented by Chow et al. (2024), Brzustowicz
(2023), and Tang & Jiang (2025) are not primarily failures of
topic identification—they are failures of rule application. The
models produce unauthorized heading forms, omit required sub-
divisions, use deprecated subfield practices, and fail to verify
headings against authority files.
A key

summary.text: Present contribution. The author argues that prior LLM failures are failures of rule application, not topic identification: unauthorised forms, missing subdivisions, deprecated subfield practice and no authority checks. Every earlier LLM study treated subject assignment as a single step, without chain-of-thought or staged reasoning, whereas catalogers move through distinct stages (aboutness, choosing topics, authority checking, building strings). The paper therefore splits the workflow into agent skills that pass structured, inspectable outputs between stages, described as externalised chain-of-thought. Unlike XMTC it needs no training data; unlike single-prompt approaches it encodes SHM rules at each stage; unlike validation-only approaches it covers the whole workflow. The system was built with Claude Code and its agent-skill framework; four skills were written from eleven LC policy documents and one review article and tested on ten books across the humanities, social sciences, sciences and fiction.
Only the section number 2.1 (the start of the methodology), with no other text.

blocks.title: Source Material and Skill Construction
blocks.content:
The four agent skills were constructed through close reading
and systematic encoding of eleven Library of Congress pol-
icy documents, listed in Table 1. These PDFs, obtained from
the Library of Congress Cataloging and Acquisitions division,
served as the primary normative source for the rules embedded
in each skill.
In addition to the LC policy documents, the conceptual anal-
ysis skill drew on Holley & Joudrey (2021), a review article
that synthesizes the theoretical frameworks for aboutness de-
termination and conceptual analysis in library and information
science. Their presentation of Wil

summary.text: Section 2.1, source material and skill construction. The four skills were built by close reading of eleven Library of Congress policy documents (listed in Table 1) and, for conceptual analysis, Holley and Joudrey's (2021) review, which supplies Wilson's four methods of subject determination, Langridge's three questions and the Joudrey–Taylor concept-identification framework. Each document's rules, exceptions, criteria and examples were translated into a SKILL.md file with terminology, decision steps, output formats and validation checks. The SKILL.md files and the Python authority-validation scripts are published on GitHub (choweric/subject-indexing-skills).

summary.text: Section 2.2, the four-skill pipeline, with Figure 1 and Table 1. Skill 1 (conceptual analysis) takes title, abstract and table of contents and applies Wilson's methods and Langridge's questions to over-generate candidate concepts with an aboutness statement. Skill 2 (quantitative filtering) applies SHM H 180: the 20% rule, the rule of three (four or more subtopics get only the broader heading), specificity, depth of indexing and ordering by predominance (H 80), and routes form concepts to LCGFT 655 fields under the 2026 policy. Skill 3 (authority validation) checks LCSH and LCGFT candidates against a local TF-IDF index built from id.loc.gov files (about 1.01 million subject headings and 8,600 genre/form terms) and names against the LC suggest2 API, avoiding the 44 GB LCNAF file of over 12 million records; it suggests authorised forms for variants and checks geographic subdivision under H 830. Skill 4 (MARC 6xx synthesis) builds fields in the H 1075 subdivision order ($a, $z, $x, $y), applies indirect geographic subdivision, drops $v, and applies H 405 and H 430 to name headings. Table 1 maps the eleven documents (H 80 to J 110 and the January 2026 LC memo) to skills.

blocks.title: Test Corpus
blocks.content:
Ten titles were selected to represent a range of disciplines,
publication types, and subject indexing challenges (Table 2).
The titles were sampled from the Harvard Library Bibliographic
Dataset (Harvard Library, 2022), an open-access collection of
over 12.7 million MARC XML bibliographic records exported
from Harvard Library’s Alma integrated library system. The
dataset, released pursuant to Harvard Library’s Open Metadata
Policy, provides a snapshot of all active bibliographic records
with one or more active holdings. For each sampled title, we
extracted the existing LCSH assignments from th

summary.text: Section 2.3, test corpus. Ten titles from varied disciplines and indexing challenges (Table 2) were sampled from the Harvard Library Bibliographic Dataset, an open collection of over 12.7 million MARC XML records exported from Harvard's Alma system under its Open Metadata Policy. The existing LCSH in each record's 6XX fields serve as the human baseline, giving ten paired comparisons. The titles' metadata (title, abstract, table of contents, ISBN, publisher) is published as a spreadsheet in the project repository with the skill files and pipeline transcripts.

blocks.title: Evaluation Method
blocks.content:
For each of the ten paired titles, the agent pipeline’s MARC
output was compared with the Harvard/LC headings along
four dimensions: (1) conceptual recall—did the agent iden-
tify the same broad topics as the human indexer? (2) heading
precision—did the agent select the correct authorized heading
form? (3) subdivision accuracy—did the agent construct subdi-
visions ($x, $z, $y) correctly? (4) genre/form treatment—did
the agent assign LCGFT 655 fields appropriately?
Because the baseline headings were captured from a live
ILS that may reflect subject indexing decisions made years
or decades ago—

summary.text: Section 2.4, evaluation method. For each title the pipeline's MARC output was compared with the Harvard/LC headings on conceptual recall, heading precision (correct authorised form), subdivision accuracy ($x, $z, $y) and genre/form treatment (LCGFT 655). Because the baseline records may reflect decisions made years earlier under different LC policies, differences are not automatically errors, and the comparison is interpretive rather than strictly quantitative.

summary.text: Section 3.1, the heading-by-heading comparison, with Tables 2 and 3. The ten titles range from Renaissance poetry, emergency-medicine fiction, race at Ford, Yunus's Banker to the Poor and currency economics to respiratory virology, artificial black holes, Richard Baxter's theology, American stand-up comedy and Andean ritual in Bolivia. Highlights: Title 1 matched the first heading exactly but assigned 3 headings against 6; Title 2 applied the 2026 policy (LCGFT Short stories and Medical fiction) where the baseline appended "Fiction"; Title 3 used broader Race discrimination and country-level geography but added Ford Motor Company and Fordism; Title 5 was the closest match; Title 6 was far more specific than the baseline's Medicine and Immunology; Title 7 missed the baseline's Mathematical models subdivision; Title 8 produced a 600 name-title heading for Baxter's Methodus theologiae; Title 10 added a chronological 651 heading (Bolivia, Politics and government, 2006-) but stopped at country level where the baseline subdivided to Toracari, and used one population group where the baseline used two.

blocks.title: Patterns Observed
blocks.content:
Specificity. In seven of ten cases, the agent produced head-
ings at a comparable or more specific level than the baseline
record. The most striking example is the medical virology ti-
tle (#6), where the agent assigned influenza-specific headings
while the baseline used broad disciplinary terms. In two cases
(Ford, black holes), the baseline was clearly more specific—
particularly in geographic granularity and topical subdivisions.
The Bolivia title presents a mixed picture: the agent added a
chronological subdivision ($y2006-) and a disciplinary head-
ing (Political anthropology) absent from

summary.text: Section 3.2, patterns observed. In seven of ten titles the agent was as specific as or more specific than the baseline, most strikingly for virology; the baseline was clearly more specific for the Ford and black-holes titles, and Bolivia was mixed. The agent assigned 600 or 610 name headings in four titles, while the baseline records had none. It consistently applied the February 2026 LCGFT policy, which the author calls the largest systematic difference and a matter of policy change rather than error. Baseline records carry more subdivisions, especially geographic, and the author suggests the synthesis skill needs guidance on subdividing below country level. Several differences (Race discrimination against Racism in the workplace, Poverty against Rural poor) are normal inter-cataloger variation, and the Bolivia title suggests the conceptual-analysis skill should look for overlapping population groups.

blocks.title: Strengths of the Agent Skill Approach
blocks.content:
The modular pipeline design offers several advantages over
monolithic prompting:
Separation of concerns. Each skill addresses one phase of
the subject indexing process, mirroring the cognitive stages a
trained subject cataloger moves through. This decomposition
makes each stage auditable: a reviewer can identify exactly
where a questionable heading decision originated.
Policy updateability. When LC policy changes—as it did in
February 2026 with the discontinuation of form subdivisions—
the change can be implemented by modifying the relevant
skill(s) without rebuilding the entire system. The 20

summary.text: Section 4.1, strengths of the agent-skill approach. Separation of concerns makes each stage auditable, so a reviewer can see where a questionable heading came from. Policy changes can be made by editing the relevant skills: the 2026 LCGFT transition touched two of the four. Each skill outputs its justifications (20% calculations, authority match scores, subdivision checks), making the reasoning inspectable. SHM rules are encoded explicitly at section level rather than learned, so every heading decision can be traced to a policy document.

blocks.title: Limitations and Areas for Improvement
blocks.content:
Geographic and chronological subdivision. The agent under-
subdivided in several cases. Strengthening the MARC synthesis
skill’s guidance on when to append $z and $y subdivisions—
particularly for works with clear geographic or temporal scope—
would address this gap.
Heading selection among synonymous terms. When multi-
ple authorized headings cover overlapping territory (e.g., Race
discrimination vs. Racism in the workplace), the agent some-
times selected the broader term. Enhanced BT/NT navigation
in the authority validation skill could guide toward the most
specific applicable heading.
Abs

summary.text: Section 4.2, limitations. The agent under-applied geographic and chronological subdivisions, which stronger guidance in the synthesis skill could fix. Among overlapping authorised headings it sometimes chose the broader term, which better broader/narrower navigation in the validation skill could address. It works from title page and abstract without consulting existing records in shared catalogues such as WorldCat, and an ISBN lookup step could improve consistency. Ten comparisons are too few for statistical generalisation, with one or two titles per discipline; the author proposes a larger stratified sample from the Harvard dataset and inter-cataloger agreement baselines.

blocks.title: Comparison Baseline Considerations
blocks.content:
The Harvard Library bibliographic dataset serves as a conve-
nient but imperfect baseline. Subject headings in a production
ILS may reflect varying levels of cataloging (full, core, mini-
mal), copy cataloging from diverse sources with differing sub-
ject indexing practices, legacy headings predating current SHM
instructions, and batch processing or automated enrichment.
The baseline headings should therefore be understood as one
professional interpretation rather than a gold standard.
5

summary.text: Section 4.3, the baseline. Headings in a production catalogue may reflect full, core or minimal cataloguing, copy cataloguing from varied sources, legacy headings predating current SHM rules, or automated enrichment, so the Harvard headings are one professional interpretation rather than a gold standard.

blocks.title: Conclusion
blocks.content:
This study demonstrates that a modular agent skill pipeline can
produce LCSH subject heading assignments that are conceptu-
ally aligned with professional subject indexing practice. The
system’s strengths—specificity, named entity identification, and
adherence to current LC policy—complement its weaknesses in
subdivision completeness and synonym navigation. The agent
skill architecture offers a practical framework for encoding
complex subject indexing rules in a maintainable, auditable,
and updateable form. It is important to note that the pipeline
addresses only the subject indexing component

summary.text: Conclusion and references. The author concludes that the modular pipeline produces LCSH assignments conceptually aligned with professional practice, strong on specificity, named entities and current LC policy, weaker on subdivision completeness and synonym choice. It covers only subject indexing (MARC 6XX), not descriptive cataloguing, classification or name authority control. Two uses are proposed, enriching records with missing or minimal headings and clearing backlogs, always as drafts for a cataloger to review. The structural finding, that decomposition into policy-grounded skills is a viable way to apply LLMs to complex knowledge work, is given most weight; against the 26–35% alignment of single-prompt approaches, the pipeline showed conceptual overlap on over half of heading comparisons. Future work: a larger corpus, copy-cataloguing consultation, and other vocabularies (MeSH, AAT, FAST). The nine references cover Kratt, Brzustowicz, Chow and colleagues, the Harvard dataset, Holley and Joudrey, the two D'Souza papers, Annif and Tang and Jiang.
